summary:
Negeri Sembilan stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors.

Every one of Malaysia's 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those state offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor in Negeri Sembilan is exposed to the Penal Code rather than to the Sharia layer.

Negeri Sembilan is the state whose cross-dressing offence was struck down on the record. In November 2014 the Court of Appeal declared section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 of Negeri Sembilan unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution. The Federal Court has more recently struck down Sharia criminal-code provisions in Selangor and Kelantan on the ground that state legislatures lack criminal-law power.

That litigation has not loosened the federal layer. Federal criminalisation of same-sex conduct persists under sections 377A and 377B, and a crackdown involving arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment has run since the 2018 election. The documented pattern of enforcement nationally is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than the individual stopping of foreign visitors, who are rarely targeted.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022 from interviews with 73 people conducted between 2018 and 2021 including people living in Negeri Sembilan, document state-sponsored discrimination and criminalisation of LGBT people in Malaysia and state that every state and the federal territories have Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct. They call on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon 'rehabilitation' programmes and rhetoric.
tangentialFactors:
Negeri Sembilan sits at the favourable end of a national pattern rather than outside it. Its section 66 was voided in 2014, yet the same cross-dressing offences remain on the books in every other state and in the federal territories, and the Federal Court's later rulings in Selangor and Kelantan rest on the division of legislative power rather than on any judgment that the prohibitions are compatible with fundamental rights.

The direction of travel at the federal level runs the other way. Human Dignity Trust's Malaysia profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records a crackdown since the 2018 election that has produced arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment under the Penal Code, so the removal of a state offence does not indicate a general easing of exposure.

The Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters research draws on interviews with 73 people across 2018 to 2021, a period covering the federal crackdown, and its recommendations address lawmakers nationwide rather than the Negeri Sembilan state assembly alone.
localsOnly:
Residents of Negeri Sembilan who are Muslim remain subject to the Sharia layer generally even though section 66 itself was struck down; enforcement of state Sharia offences is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and those laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

People living in Negeri Sembilan were among those interviewed for the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters documentation of state-sponsored discrimination, published 10 August 2022, which covers employment, healthcare, education and encounters with officials as well as criminal liability.

The report calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon 'rehabilitation' programmes and rhetoric, targets that would sit with the Malaysian Parliament and the state legislative assembly rather than with visitors.
